title: The attacker comes back
briefing: svc_backup's password was rotated an hour ago. If the attacker still has a foothold anywhere, they will try the account again soon, and you want to see it the moment it happens, not in tomorrow's report.
A live copy of the auth log is being written to `live/secure` right now. Follow it and catch the attacker's first new attempt.

lesson.p: `tail` prints the end of a file. With `-f` (follow) it keeps the file open and prints each new line as it is written, until you press Ctrl+C. Pipe it into `grep` to watch for one thing.

flags: everything from line 5 to the end; `-n +1` is the whole file
follow: print new lines as they arrive. Ctrl+C stops it.
follow the NAME, not the open file: keeps going after logrotate replaces the file. Use this on real logs.
stop after the first match; the pipeline ends instead of waiting forever
print each match at once. Without it, grep holds output back in a block when it writes into another pipe.
kill CMD after 30 seconds (exit status 124): a safe way to follow for a while in a script

lesson.note: The feed starts when you open this quest, writes a few lines straight away, then one every few seconds. Press Reset files to start it again from the top.
`tail -f FILE | grep X | cut ...` can look stuck: grep buffers its output when it is not writing to the terminal, so `cut` sees nothing until grep's buffer fills. `grep --line-buffered` fixes it.

examples.title: The end of a file

stages.why: The last three lines: the most recent events in a log that is written in time order.

examples.output:
Mar 13 09:20:44 web-01 sshd[2260]: Failed password for ops_bob from 198.51.100.22 port 51544 ssh2
Mar 13 09:20:51 web-01 sshd[2260]: Accepted password for ops_bob from 198.51.100.22 port 51544 ssh2
Mar 13 09:30:12 web-01 su[2302]: pam_unix(su-l:session): session opened for user root(uid=0) by ops_bob(uid=1002)

examples.title: From a line number to the end

stages.why: A plus sign means "starting at line 9", not "the last 9". Useful to skip a header: `tail -n +2 file.csv`.

examples.title: Follow for a while, then stop

stages.why: Print the last two lines, then wait for more. Nothing is writing to this file, so nothing else appears.
Stop tail after two seconds instead of pressing Ctrl+C.
124 is timeout's way of saying "I had to kill it". Scripts can test for it.

examples.title: Follow until the first match
examples.command: tail -n +1 -f training/secure.log | grep -m1 Accepted; echo done

stages.why: Read the whole file from the top, then keep following.
grep exits after the first match. tail notices that nobody is reading any more and exits too, so the shell moves on to `echo done`.

examples.output:
Mar 13 09:10:01 web-01 sshd[2101]: Accepted publickey for ops_alice from 198.51.100.21 port 50122 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:k3Fq0example
done

examples.title: A follow pipeline that does not stall
examples.command: timeout 2 tail -f training/secure.log | grep --line-buffered Failed | cut -d' ' -f9-

stages.why: Pass each failed login on immediately, instead of in a block.
Everything from field 9 on: who, from where, on which port.

examples.output:
invalid user admin from 203.0.113.9 port 40001 ssh2
root from 203.0.113.9 port 40007 ssh2
invalid user test from 203.0.113.9 port 40013 ssh2
ops_bob from 198.51.100.22 port 51544 ssh2

challenge.question: Follow live/secure. When 203.0.113.66 tries to log in again, what source port is its first new attempt coming from?

hints: Start following before the attempt arrives: `tail -f live/secure`. Watch for the attacker's address, then read the port off the line. Ctrl+C when you have it.
Let the pipeline wait for you: `tail -f live/secure | grep -m1 203.0.113.66` prints the first matching line and exits. `grep -oE 'port [0-9]+'` then pulls out the port.

why: The attacker tried svc_backup twice and gave up: the rotated password held. That they came back at all means they kept the credential, and probably a list of other hosts where it might work. Rotate it everywhere the account exists, not just here.

On a RHEL host, `journalctl -f -u sshd` follows the same events from the journal, and `journalctl -f -u sshd --grep '203.0.113.66'` filters them. On a host that writes files, use `tail -F`: logrotate renames `secure` at night, and `-f` would keep following the old, renamed file.

Watching by hand does not scale. The same idea, automated, is fail2ban (`dnf install fail2ban`, the sshd jail) or a SIEM rule: match the pattern, then act. You just did by hand what those tools do in a loop.
